claims.text: Combining DSC, CALPHAD modeling, and in-situ neutron imaging can accurately and efficiently determine melting temperature, fusion enthalpy and entropy, melting volume change, and liquid-phase thermodynamic properties across a broad range of high-entropy alloys.
Controlled DSC ramps can detect fusion transitions in the alloys.
CALPHAD calculations can predict the relevant thermodynamic behavior of high-entropy alloys.
In-situ neutron imaging during melting can validate liquid-state mixing and phase stability.
The approach is primarily applicable to simple FCC or BCC high-entropy alloys over temperatures from room temperature to above melting.
Latent-heat peaks and volume changes observed during melting mediate the transition from an ordered solid to a disordered liquid.
Configurational entropy influences melting behavior.
Short-range order can influence melting behavior.
Abrupt heat-capacity increases and endothermic DSC peaks denote fusion.
DSC observations can be correlated with CALPHAD-modeled Gibbs free-energy changes that include configurational and thermal entropy contributions.
In-situ neutron imaging can measure volume changes during melting.
In-situ neutron imaging provides spatially resolved verification by capturing the merging of phase-separated regions in the liquid.
The combined approach will reduce errors by approximately 15–20% relative to traditional single-technique methods.
DSC transitions will be distinct and reproducible and will align quantitatively with CALPHAD predictions.
Neutron imaging will reveal liquid-phase homogenization events that confirm the predicted thermodynamic behavior.
Standalone DSC and conventional phase-diagram assessments generally have lower accuracy and efficiency in complex multicomponent systems.
The approach is most applicable to high-temperature single-phase alloys and may be less effective for alloys with multiple intermetallic phases.
CALPHAD precision for some high-entropy-alloy systems is limited by database reliability.
Unaccounted short-range ordering or kinetic barriers during melting can introduce measurement uncertainty.
The approach is designated as falsified if at least one measured quantity differs from its CALPHAD prediction by more than about 20% and imaging also fails to show the expected liquid homogenization.
